extracted.intended_audience: students, historians, and general readers interested in the history and practices of early newspaper advertising
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and illustrates the practical conventions, pricing, rhetoric, and examples of newspaper advertising in the late 17th and early 18th centuries in Britain, using reproduced advertisements and commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertisement length and typical form
rubrics_metrics.description: Long advertisements were unknown; they generally averaged about eight lines of narrow measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early newspaper notices were short (≈8 lines); long ads developed later. Example: the book notes that first advertisements were so few that no notice was called for, and the average was about eight lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pricing per advertisement (fixed fee)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paid for at about a shilling each (for an average advertisement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical early pricing around the turn of the century was roughly one shilling per advertisement, subject to fluctuations by paper and period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Per-line charging and rate statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Some papers charged by the line — e.g., the County Gentleman's Courant: 'the price of advertisements is advanced to twopence per line.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers varied pricing models; per-line charging emerged and was explicitly stated in some journals' copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Per-item and renewal fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain specialty journals gave itemized charges — e.g., 'a shilling for a horse or coach for notification, and sixpence for renewing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Niche papers (e.g., for horses/second-hand coaches) used bespoke rates and renewal fees; advertisers needed to follow those rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stating charges in the paper (notice of rates)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plan of stating charges became common: some papers had notices of price per advertisement stated at foot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers began printing their advertisement rates in-column or at foot to standardize billing and inform advertisers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow paper-specific rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Various rules obtained upon various papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each journal had its own conventions (length, format, rates, renewals); advertisers had to conform to the host paper's rules and customs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of testimonials and faith-based persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Vendors of ointment and pills published testimonials 'from time immemorial' — 'faith will move mountains' — using testimonials to claim cures and success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testimonial culture was a staple of medical/quack advertising; advertisers relied on published 'cases' to persuade credulous customers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guarantee wording and scope ('No cure no pay')
rubrics_metrics.description: Example advertisement: 'No cure no money.' (used by a lunacy-curer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guarantees were used to build trust but often had limited scope — the text notes the 'no cure no pay' referred only to lunacy cases and not to dropsy, illustrating careful (and sometimes restrictive) wording of guarantees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puffery and hyperbolic claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers sometimes made extravagant assertions — e.g., a microscope 'which magnified objects more than two million times' and 'spectacles by which objects might be discovered at twenty or thirty miles' distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyperbole and grandiose claims were common (puffing). Such claims were rhetorically potent but risked provoking rebuttal from competitors and public skepticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public rebuttal, demonstration, and wagers to settle claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Competitors used public notices to challenge claims and offered demonstrations and wagers (e.g., Yarwell & Sterrop offering to demonstrate and stake Guineas against Willdey & Brandreth's claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When extraordinary product claims appeared, rivals resorted to public comparisons, demonstrations, and bets to prove insufficiency or superiority — an early form of adversarial quality testing in the press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of factual precision and attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Disputes arose over claims of invention/credit and alleged falsehoods in advertisements (masters accusing apprentices of 'fraudently appropriating' inventions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisers were exposed to reputational attack; factual accuracy about provenance and capability affected credibility and could provoke 'newspaper warfare'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of free literature or treatises as inducement
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers offered gratis material — e.g., 'we are now writing a small treatise ... which will be given gratis to our customers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing free explanatory literature or treatises was used as an inducement and to lend a veneer of learned authority to the seller's wares.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience targeting and tiered pricing by social quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: 'Every one is to pay according to his quality from one guinea to 4 guineas per month' and special consideration 'for poor Gent, and Ladies'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisers tailored offers and prices according to the social status of clientele (tiered rates, special offers), and explicitly addressed different audiences in copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event/program detail and benefit announcements for theatres
rubrics_metrics.description: Theatrical ads listed specific plays, parts, new entries, dances, singers, and noted benefits (e.g., benefit of 'a gentleman in great distress' to relieve his family).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theatre advertising gave detailed program information, performers' names, special features, and philanthropic/benefit reasons to attract audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include location, times and contact/address for traceability
rubrics_metrics.description: Most notices gave addresses and times (e.g., physicians with charges and visiting fees, schools with addresses); the absence of such detail (e.g., the stews ad with no name or address) made an ad notably vague.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit location, hours, and contact details increased an advertisement's utility and credibility; omission could leave the notice untraceable or informal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising as a multi-purpose communication medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising had become recognised for 'the conveniencies of trade, but for political, lovemaking, fortune-hunting, swindling, and the thousand and one other purposes' in a large community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early newspapers functioned as platforms for a wide array of social communication beyond simple commerce; advertisers exploited the medium for diverse aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialty/niche advertising practices (raffles, lotteries, sales)
rubrics_metrics.description: Raffle advertisements and notices of lotteries ('sales' where the only things sold were most likely the confiding speculators) were frequent; many kinds of items were raffled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain categories of commerce (lotteries, raffles) developed characteristic ad styles and vocabulary; advertisers in these niches followed established customs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims of professional credentials and pricing transparency for services
rubrics_metrics.description: Service providers (e.g., a physician 'a Graduate in the University of Oxford, and of many years standing') published credentials and set transparent fees (e.g., sixpence for an account of disease; two shillings sixpence visit in London).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listing formal qualifications and clear fees in advertisements served to legitimise professional service providers and differentiate them from quacks.
